subtitle: The connecting words of written German, and two-part connectors
words.intro: The Ruhr was coal and steel for 150 years. The last deep mine closed in 2018. Now a huge colliery in Essen is a UNESCO site with a design museum, and every family round here has a story about a grandfather underground.

grammar[0].fact: *Freilich* in Bavaria just means *of course*: *Ja, freilich!* In the north, and in writing, it means *admittedly*. It’s one small word that can start a quarrel, and it’s why you should listen for where someone comes from.

grammar[1].fact: From the late 1950s West Germany brought in workers from Turkey, Italy, Greece and elsewhere. Many went underground in the Ruhr. It’s why a *Trinkhalle* in Duisburg may run on Turkish tea, and why the region’s football clubs have always had their own idea of who’s local.

document.intro: A real sign at the site of a long-gone colliery in Dortmund, put up by volunteers. It’s a little history in the written past and the passive. Follow the dates. *Stillgelegt* means shut down, *die Teufe* is miners’ German for depth.
document.fact: Hammer and mallet, crossed, is the miners’ sign, and you’ll see it on railway stations and town crests all over the Ruhr. Volunteers have put up plates like this one at closed pits, so that some memory stays when the buildings have gone.

reading.intro: Lena’s grandfather, Opa Heinz, was a miner in Essen for thirty-four years. Max is writing about the Ruhr for his evening course, and he’s reading aloud what he has written. Opa Heinz has his feet up, and he has heard all of this before.
reading.photos[1].caption: Auf die Halde steigen: Was unten lag, ist jetzt ein Berg.
reading.fact: *Glück auf!* is the miners’ greeting: it wishes you good luck in finding a vein, and a safe return. When Germany’s last deep coal mine in Bottrop closed in December 2018, miners handed the president the last piece of coal. People across the Ruhr still say it, at funerals and at football.
